name: Nora Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers or AI firms. This is confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach cello at the community centre, arrange simple parts for a youth quartet, edit audition tapes and play weekend weddings when they book us. My music bachelor's helps with the scores, and I use AI every day for drafts and reminders, though I still check each note with a student.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household leaning on right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Leila works at a nursery, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. The music pay is low, there are few similar jobs nearby, and we have under a month's expenses saved.

say: I'd welcome **quicker invoices** while keeping my lessons and live quartet dates.
I'd tell colleagues that **playing together** still earns the wedding fee.
think: Our **three-week cushion** leaves the mortgage exposed to ordinary cancellations.
Daily **AI reminders** save time but do not guarantee another paid date.
do: Confirm **twelve centre hours** for next term this week.
Keep the **two booked weddings** and delay recording cables until both fees clear and the mortgage is covered.
feel: I feel **anxious** because a small booking loss could drain our savings.
S0.quote: An encouraging client message will not pay for our children's school trip.
fieldNote: Her **three-week reserve** explains baseline anxiety despite steady teaching hours.
She uses **AI daily** for small tasks, while the household still depends on confirmed fees.

steps.text: Confirm twelve centre teaching hours for next term
Keep two booked quartet wedding dates
Delay recording cables until both wedding fees clear and mortgage is covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the studio that a quicker invoice is welcome, but the strings still need a bow and a player. My Tuesday pupils and the weekend wedding quartet would carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI daily to sort practice reminders and draft simple lesson sheets, but that hasn't made our mortgage smaller. We have barely three weeks of expenses saved, and my partner Leila's nursery wage covers food more reliably than my wedding dates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the centre to confirm next term's twelve teaching hours and keep the two booked quartet dates. If both weddings pay, I'll put forty from each fee into the mortgage envelope before buying more recording cables.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, even when nothing dramatic changes. A cancelled wedding and one lost pupil would use up the little we have put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did a moved wedding cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One wedding moved last summer and I taught an extra Sunday lesson to cover the utility bill. I can do that once, but I cannot build a family's budget on emergency lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need before paying for the school trip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show Leila the centre email before we decide on the children's school trip. We would put the deposit aside only after a fee actually clears. An encouraging client message will not pay for our children's school trip.

say: I'd bring **paid-hour records** to the musicians association.
I'd ask for **family consent** before any new tool handles pupil recordings.
think: **Arranging and editing** make a quarter of my pay and could shrink.
The centre may keep pupils but cut **paid preparation**, putting the mortgage at risk.
do: Compare **twelve weeks of invoices** with two tutors at the association this month.
Offer a **strings class** after a quarter preparation-pay loss only with signed room/pay terms, ten paid places and confirmed pickup.
Keep **current lessons** while any new class proves its paid demand.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because a lost paid day could delay the mortgage.
S1.quote: A full classroom is no use if the preparation hours are unpaid.
fieldNote: She pairs **association records** with an enrolment-gated class, using her adaptive outlook without risking mortgage money.
Her **pupil recordings** require family consent; daily AI use does not imply permission to upload them.

steps.text: Compare twelve weeks of invoices with tutors at musicians association
Offer class after quarter preparation-pay loss: signed room/pay, ten paid places covering teaching/preparation, confirmed pickup
Keep existing lessons while testing paid group demand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the centre tutors to ask how many paid lesson-planning and recording hours the new tools remove. I would bring our figures to the musicians association before the manager writes a flat fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A quarter of my pay comes from arranging, editing audition tapes and writing practice notes. AI can do much of that quickly, and the centre might keep the children while cutting my paid preparation hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll collect twelve weeks of invoices and compare them with two colleagues at the association. In the first year of change, if preparation pay falls by a quarter, I'll offer a small-group strings class only with signed room and teaching-fee terms, ten paid places covering preparation and teaching, and Leila confirming pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because even one fewer paid day could make the mortgage late. I can organise quickly, but a meeting isn't another wage. A full classroom is no use if the preparation hours are unpaid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the Thursday room actually yours to use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre has an empty room on Thursdays, but the manager has not offered it to me. I'd ask for written room terms and a set fee before telling parents there is a class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Whose recordings would you use to test a new tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not send pupils' recordings into a new editing tool without their families' permission. My own rough takes are fine for tests, but a child's playing belongs to the child.

say: I'd seek written **2028 centre hours** and recording rights.
I'd keep **booked quartet work** while humans still play the weddings.
think: **AGI in 2028** threatens editing before robot players arrive around 2031.
Leila's **nursery wage** cannot cover the mortgage if centre preparation pay halves.
do: Request an **autumn hours plan** and list last year's arranging fees now.
Review **written total interest** with Leila before accepting mortgage relief if preparation hours halve in the first year after 2028.
Keep **twelve teaching hours** until a qualifying posted library job offers replacement net pay after travel and confirmed pickup.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because three weeks saved cannot fund a long job search.
S2.quote: The quartet may keep its weddings while my paid desk hours disappear.
fieldNote: She sees **thinking-work loss** in 2028 before robots can play around 2031.
Both **mortgage options** and library work remain conditional on full costs, a real vacancy and replacement pay.

steps.text: Request written autumn hours; keep twelve teaching hours until qualifying written job offer
Review written total interest with Leila before relief if preparation halves after 2028
Apply after 2028: qualifying posted library role, confirmed pickup, written net-after-travel pay replacing loss

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the quartet that 2028 is close enough to get every fee and recording right in writing. I would keep playing weddings while couples still choose us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could arrange, edit and prepare lessons better and cheaper than I can. Robot players come around 2031, so the quartet may still work for a few years, but the paid desk hours could vanish first; Leila's wage alone will not pay the mortgage. The quartet may keep its weddings while my paid desk hours disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the centre for a written autumn hours plan and list each arranging fee from the past year. In the first year after 2028, if preparation hours halve, I'll ask the credit union about a temporary mortgage plan and apply for a posted library music-room job only if its net pay after travel replaces those hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed, but I can still make a list and call people. Our three-week savings will not carry a long search for the few local jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check before accepting mortgage relief?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The credit union might extend a payment, but I would ask for the total extra interest before agreeing. Leila and I would read the terms together before signing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the library job available now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The library job was advertised last year and may never open again. I'd check that my degree qualifies and Leila can cover pickup, and keep the twelve teaching hours until a written offer replaces the lost pay after travel.

say: I'd offer **paid ensemble time** rather than a free showcase.
I'd ask the centre for a **signed fee** and enough safe loan instruments.
think: **AGI in 2031** threatens scores before robots play around 2034.
**Editing fees** could shrink earlier, so our household pay is at risk now.
do: Pitch a **six-week group** with signed room/fee, working instruments, teacher safety check and twelve prepayments covering every player.
Refund **deposits** if fewer than twelve pay and keep individual pupils.
Continue the **group** in first year after 2031 only if twelve renew and fee covers room and players.
feel: I feel **anxious** because tape fees may fall before the class grows.
S3.quote: I won't pay the centre to let me teach.
fieldNote: Her **twelve-family gate** and borrowed safe instruments avoid using mortgage money for a new class.
She tests **AI drafts** but relies on a teacher and room check before bringing children together.

steps.text: Pitch group: signed room/fee, working instruments, teacher safety-check and twelve prepayments covering players
Refund deposits if fewer than twelve families pay
Continue group first year after 2031 if twelve renew and fees cover players and room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell parents five years is time to build an ensemble their children want to attend every week. I would ask for paid room time and not promise a free class to win applause.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 could do my scores and lesson plans, and robot players may arrive around 2034. But ordinary editing tools could cut my paid tape work before then, so the extra years do not leave the mortgage untouched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I'll pitch a six-week family strings session only with a signed fee, a loaned room, working instruments, another teacher's safety check and twelve prepayments covering every player. By 2031 I'll try a second term only if the first pays for every player; in the first year after AGI, I'll keep it only if twelve families renew and the fee still clears room and player costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because I can test a small class over five years, but the tape fees may go sooner. I won't pay the centre to let me teach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who provides the instruments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the centre's loan instruments if they have enough in working order. If only eight families pay, I'd return deposits and keep the individual lessons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check the group is safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask another teacher to check the group plan before I book it. I use AI for drafts, but I still need to know whether twelve children can play safely in that room.

say: I'd try **regular local music** with paid families and players.
I'd insist the **centre pays tutors** who teach the next generation.
think: At **53**, I need work when AGI arrives in 2036.
**Early editing losses** and robots around 2039 could weaken both desk and live fees.
do: Ask the **arts hall** for written room and insurance costs before announcing a workshop.
Run **workshops** with ten deposits covering all costs; continue after 2036 only with ten renewals, saving spare proceeds toward three months.
Keep **centre hours** until a posted school role gives written net pay covering travel and childcare.
feel: I feel **anxious** because current mortgage bills make a decade's warning incomplete protection.
S4.quote: Ten deposits are a plan; ten people saying they'll come are not.
fieldNote: She builds a **conditional live workshop** rather than borrowing against a future audience.
A **written school offer** would have to cover travel and childcare before she leaves centre hours.

steps.text: Run workshops with written rates and ten deposits; renew after 2036 only if all costs covered
Keep centre hours until posted school role offers written net pay covering childcare and travel
Aim for three months saved by 2036 from spare paid workshop proceeds after household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our quartet that a decade gives us time to make regular local music rather than chase one-off edits. I would also ask the centre to pay whoever teaches the next generation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 when AGI arrives in 2036, retirement is too far away to solve this. Robot players follow around 2039, but tape editing could fade well before 2036, so I need reliable teaching and booked live work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask the town arts hall about a monthly paid quartet workshop only if it signs the room rate and ten families prepay enough for room, insurance and players. By 2036 I'll aim for three months of expenses saved from spare proceeds after household bills; in the first year after AGI, I'll continue only if ten renewals still cover every cost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because we have a mortgage now, not after a decade. A long runway helps me try small paid nights without promising the children a new income yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What has to be covered before you announce a Sunday date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall manager has said there may be room on Sundays, but hasn't given a price. I would not announce a date until the room rate, insurance and player fees are covered by the ten deposits. Ten deposits are a plan; ten people saying they'll come are not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the centre for another school?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a new school post opens nearer home, I would consider it only with a written pay offer that covers childcare and travel. I would not abandon the twelve centre hours for an interview.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because editing and arranging pay could disappear before I can replace it locally. A written centre schedule, full-cost mortgage terms and a genuinely open job paying after travel would help us act before arrears.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns a child's rehearsal recording once a tool has touched it. I would ask a child's family before uploading a rehearsal recording, even if the software promises to help.

headlineQuote: I would ask a child's family before uploading a rehearsal recording, even if the software promises to help.
portrait: Nora is a **43-year-old** experienced cello teacher with a music bachelor's, recording work and wedding quartet dates.
She uses **AI daily** but has low pay, few local music jobs, two children and less than one month's savings.
She expects **editing and arranging** fees to fall before robots reach live performance three years after AGI.
She tests **paid group classes** with written room and fee terms, prepaid families and safe loan instruments.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because desk-based music fees could vanish before local replacement work appears.
whatWouldHelp: A **written centre schedule**, clear mortgage costs and a real net-paying vacancy would help her avoid arrears.
